planting.note: Plant offsets or container divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Rosularia spreads by short stolons and establishes quickly in rock garden crevices or shallow troughs.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky mountain slopes of its native Caucasus and Middle East range. Rosularia forms tiny, tightly packed rosettes of fleshy blue-green to gray-green leaves, closely resembling a miniature Sempervivum, and spreads slowly into a dense mat by sending out short runners tipped with new offset rosettes. Clusters of small star-shaped pink or white flowers rise on short stalks above the foliage in summer, after which the flowering rosette fades while surrounding offsets carry the colony forward. It is an excellent choice for rock gardens, stone walls, and shallow alpine troughs where winter wet drainage is assured.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container divisions in spring in lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun; Spiny Orostachys is exceptionally cold-hardy but intolerant of winter wet.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun, giving it the same open rocky conditions as Sempervivum. Native across Siberia, Mongolia, and northern China, this Orostachys forms silvery gray-green rosettes with soft spine-tipped leaf margins that give the species its spiny common name, and it ranks among the most cold-tolerant of all rosette succulents. Each rosette is monocarpic, sending up a single dense flower spike of small whitish-green blooms before that rosette dies, while offset rosettes clustered around the base continue the colony indefinitely. Use it in rock gardens, gravel beds, or troughs where excellent drainage protects it through winter freeze-thaw cycles.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Orostachys spreads steadily by runners and tolerates more summer humidity than many rosette succulents.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade. Native to Japan, Korea, and parts of China, this species forms flattened rosettes of powdery, dusty blue-green leaves that often blush purple-red at the tips under strong sun and cool weather, spreading into a loose mat by short runners tipped with new rosettes. In late summer or fall, mature rosettes send up a tapering spike of small star-shaped white flowers before that rosette dies back, while the surrounding offsets keep the planting going. It suits rock gardens, gravel beds, and container plantings, tolerating more humid summer conditions than many of its rosette-succulent relatives.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun; Spotted Sedum roots readily from broken stems and tolerates light frost once established.

directions: Plant in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun to very light shade. Native to northeastern Mexico, this shrubby little succulent produces fleshy, cylindrical blue-green leaves marked with purple-maroon spotting that deepens into a rich chocolate-purple flush under bright light and dry, stressed conditions, giving the plant its common names. Clusters of small tubular yellow flowers open in late summer on older growth, and stems that break or droop root readily wherever they touch soil, making it easy to multiply. Grow it in a rock garden or container in warm climates, bringing it under cover or into a sheltered spot where winter temperatures regularly drop below the mid-20s.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Bluff Lettuce resents summer irrigation and overhead watering, which can cause rot in the powdery leaves.

directions: Plant in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to light coastal shade. Native to bluffs and rocky outcrops along the California and southern Oregon coast, Bluff Lettuce forms rosettes of thick, blunt-tipped leaves coated in a chalky white-blue powder (farina) that protects the plant from intense sun and salt spray. Rosettes clump and offset over time into dense colonies, and tall, branched flower stalks bearing small yellow blooms rise above the foliage in late spring. Keep it dry over summer and avoid overhead watering, since the powdery bloom washes off and the fleshy leaves are prone to rot in consistently damp conditions.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sea Lettuce needs a dry summer dormancy and resents soggy, heavy soil.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light coastal shade. Native to bluffs and sandy slopes along the central and southern California coast, Sea Lettuce forms substantial rosettes of fleshy, pale gray-green to chalky-blue leaves on short stems, clustering into broad colonies as offsets accumulate around older rosettes. Branched flower stalks carrying small bright yellow blooms rise well above the foliage in spring and early summer, attracting bees and butterflies. It thrives on neglect once established, going semi-dormant through the dry summer months, and needs excellent drainage above all else to avoid rot in wetter climates.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; this variegated stonecrop spreads by creeping stems and roots wherever they touch soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, which helps protect the variegated foliage from scorching in hot climates. Native to China, this low, creeping sedum bears narrow, needle-like leaves arranged in whorls along trailing stems, each leaf edged in creamy white around a soft green center, giving the whole mat a bright, airy texture distinct from the solid-gold coloring of Sedum rupestre 'Angelina'. Small star-shaped yellow flowers appear in loose clusters in summer, though the plant is grown mainly for its foliage. It spreads readily into a low groundcover for rock gardens, pathway edges, and container plantings, trimming back any all-green reversion shoots to keep the variegation strong.
